Text:
Physics is usually divided into two fields:

motion, fluids, heat, sound, light, electricity, magnetism → {{c1::classical::classical/modern}} physics

relativity, atomic structure, quantum theory, condensed matter, nuclear physics, elementary particles, cosmology and astrophysics → {{c1::modern::classical/modern}} physics
Back Extra:
Why: physics is the most basic of the sciences — it deals with the behavior and structure of matter.

Cue: the study of motion is also called mechanics.

Text: Aristotle, who argued that rest is the natural state of objects, lived {{c1::384–322 B.C.::lifespan}}, and Galileo, the first true experimentalist, lived {{c2::1564–1642::lifespan}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: Aristotle watched pushed objects slow and stop, so rest seemed natural; Galileo imagined frictionless motion continuing forever, and so founded our modern view of motion.

Cue: nearly 1,900 years separate them — B.C. antiquity to the 1600s.

Ex: Raphael's The School of Athens (c. 1510) places Aristotle at its center, in blue, beside Plato.
verified_by: agent, read from page render this run; editor: dates re-checked verbatim against idx 1/2 highlights

Text: In science, a theory is {{c1::a broad, testable explanation that organizes observations}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a law is a concise, general statement of how nature behaves — "theory" is reserved for the more general picture of the phenomena.

Why: theories are never derived directly from observations — they are inspirations of the human mind, accepted or rejected by observation and experiment.

Ex: the atomic theory — matter is made up of atoms — sprang from creative minds, not from direct observation of atoms.

Text: The notebooks of {{c1::Leonardo da Vinci}} contain the first references to {{c2::the forces acting within a structure}} — a subject regarded as physics today, with great relevance to architecture and building.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: da Vinci (1452–1519) worked a century before Galileo (1564–1642), the first true experimentalist.

Why: the development of physics has both influenced and been influenced by other fields.

Ex: early work on electricity, leading to the battery and electric current, came from Luigi Galvani — an eighteenth-century physiologist.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In science, a {{c1::model}} is {{c2::an analogy to something already familiar}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a theory is broader, more detailed, and gives quantitatively testable predictions — a model only offers structural similarity to the phenomena.

Why: the purpose of a model is an approximate mental or visual picture — something to hold on to — when we cannot see what is actually happening.

Ex: the wave model of light — we cannot see light waves, but light behaves in many respects as water waves do.
verified_by: consolidator: fact read verbatim from the page render this run

Text: A scientific {{c1::law}} is {{c2::a concise but general statement}} about how nature behaves, often taking the form of {{c3::a relationship or equation between quantities}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a principle is the same kind of statement but less general; a theory is a broader, more detailed picture of the phenomena.

Ex: conservation of electric charge; Newton's second law, F = ma.

Pitfall: scientific laws are descriptive — they say how nature does behave; political laws are prescriptive — how we ought to behave.
verified_by: consolidator: fact read verbatim from the page render this run

Text: In science, a principle is {{c1::a statement like a law, but less general}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "For less general statements, the term principle is often used (such as Archimedes' principle)."

Distinguish: a law is experimentally valid over a wide range of observed phenomena — charge conservation, F = ma; a principle covers a narrower range.

Text: Interpolate means {{c1::to estimate between a scale's smallest divisions}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "It is difficult for the observer to estimate (or 'interpolate') between the smallest divisions" — reading a board's width with a centimeter ruler.

Distinguish: to extrapolate is to estimate beyond the range of the known marks or data; interpolating stays between them.

Cue: the difficulty of interpolating between a ruler's 0.1 cm marks is why a reading carries an estimated uncertainty of about the smallest division, or half of it.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: The estimated uncertainty of a measurement is {{c1::the stated ± it might be off by}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "The width of a board might be written as 8.8 ± 0.1 cm … the ±0.1 cm ('plus or minus 0.1 cm') represents the estimated uncertainty, so that the actual width most likely lies between 8.7 and 8.9 cm."

Distinguish: the percent uncertainty is the relative version — the same ± divided by the measured value, × 100; the estimated uncertainty is the absolute ± in the measurement's own units.

Text: The {{c1::percent uncertainty}} of a measurement is {{c2::the uncertainty over the measured value, × 100}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: a measurement of 8.8 cm with an uncertainty of about 0.1 cm has a percent uncertainty of 0.1/8.8 × 100% ≈ 1%.

Distinguish: the estimated uncertainty is the absolute ± itself (e.g. ±0.1 cm); the percent uncertainty re-expresses that ± relative to the size of the measured value.
verified_by: consolidator: fact read verbatim from the page render this run

Text: When a value's uncertainty is not stated explicitly, it is assumed to be {{c1::one or a few units::amount}} in the {{c1::last digit::position}} specified.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: do not write 8.80 cm when you mean 8.8 cm — the trailing zero claims an uncertainty on the order of 0.01 cm (a width between 8.79 and 8.81 cm), when you actually believe it is between 8.7 and 8.9 cm.

Distinguish: a written ± (8.8 ± 0.1 cm) states the estimated uncertainty explicitly; the last-digit assumption is only the fallback when no ± is given.

Ex: a length given as 8.8 cm is assumed uncertain by about 0.1 or 0.2 cm.

Text: A number's {{c1::significant figures}} are its {{c2::reliably known}} digits.
Back Extra:
Ex: 23.21 cm has four significant figures; 0.062 cm has only two.

Distinguish: place-holder zeros do not count — the zeros in 0.062 are not reliably known digits, they only show where the decimal point goes.

Text: In a distance stated as "roughly 80 km" between two cities, the number of significant figures is {{c1::one}} — the zero is merely a {{c1::place holder}}.
Back Extra:
Why: only reliably known digits are significant — "roughly" says the zero is not reliably known, merely holding a place.

Cue: a bare 80 is ambiguous — the wording around it (roughly … vs. precisely …) decides how many of its digits are significant.
verified_by: editor: count and place-holder wording verbatim in the extracted highlight

Text: With no suggestion that a distance written 80 km is a rough approximation, it is often assumed accurate to within about {{c1::1 or 2 km}}, and the number of significant figures is {{c1::two}}.
Back Extra:
Why: with no hedge, every written digit — the 8 and the 0 — is taken as reliably known.

Distinguish: said as "roughly 80 km", the zero would instead be a mere place holder — the hedge, not the digits, changes the count.
verified_by: editor: 1-or-2-km tolerance and two-sig-fig count verbatim in the extracted highlight

Text: A distance of 80 km known precisely, to within ±0.1 km, is written {{c2::80.0 km::notation}} and has {{c1::three::number of sig figs}} significant figures.
Back Extra:
Why: every digit written claims to be reliably known — the trailing .0 asserts the tenths place was actually measured.

Cue: the last-digit uncertainty convention read in reverse — writing one more digit is the way to claim a smaller uncertainty.
verified_by: editor: 80.0 notation and three-sig-fig count verbatim in the extracted highlight

Text: In a multiplication or division of measured values, the final result should have no more digits than the value with the {{c1::fewest significant figures}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: adding or subtracting instead keeps the fewest decimal places — the fewest-sig-figs rule is for multiplying and dividing.

Why: the dropped digits are not significant — quoting 77 cm² implies an honest uncertainty of about 1 or 2 cm², which is all the inputs support.

Ex: 11.3 cm × 6.8 cm = 76.84 cm², but 6.8 cm has only two significant figures, so the result is rounded to 77 cm².

Text: The {{c1::precision}} of a measurement, in the strict sense, is {{c2::its repeatability using a given instrument}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: accuracy is how close a measurement comes to the true value — a ruler built with a 2% error still gives repeatable (precise) readings that are all slightly off.

Ex: measuring a board's width many times as 8.81, 8.85, 8.78, 8.82 cm shows a precision a bit better than 0.1 cm.

Text: The {{c1::accuracy}} of a measurement is {{c2::how close it is to the true value}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: precision is the repeatability of the measurement with a given instrument — high precision does not guarantee accuracy.

Ex: a ruler manufactured with a 2% error measures a board's width of about 8.8 cm to an accuracy of only about ±0.2 cm.

Cue: the estimated uncertainty you state (±) is meant to take both accuracy and precision into account.

Text: The first truly international measurement standard was the {{c1::meter::unit}}, established by the {{c2::French Academy of Sciences::institution}} in the {{c3::1790s::decade}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: a platinum rod was made to represent the chosen length — a physical object to define the meter.

Cue: one meter is, very roughly, nose to fingertip with your arm and hand stretched out horizontally.
verified_by: editor — numeric-looks warning cleared: 1790s is EXACT in idx 22's own highlight; needs_human_check derives at verify_report (R35-family convention); consolidator: fact read verbatim from the page render this run

Text: The standard meter was originally chosen to be one {{c1::ten-millionth::fraction}} of the distance from the Earth's {{c2::equator to either pole::from where to where}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the span runs equator → pole (either one), not pole to pole.

Ex: modern measurements of the Earth show the intended length was off by only about one-fiftieth of 1%.
verified_by: editor — Back Extra Ex (off by one-fiftieth of 1%) is idx 23's own † footnote; its text was captured in idx 26's context window, now cited so R13 support is auditable; consolidator: fact read verbatim from the page render this run

Text: Since 1983, the meter is defined as the length of the path traveled by {{c1::light in vacuum}} during {{c2::1/299,792,458}} of a second.
Back Extra:
Cue: the fraction is the reciprocal of the speed of light — 299,792,458 m/s was its best measured value under the old meter definition.

Pathway: a physical rod → engraved marks on a metal bar (1889) → krypton-86 wavelengths (1960) → light travel time (1983, current).
verified_by: editor — fraction 1/299,792,458 matches idx 24's context digit-for-digit (CJK slash normalized); Pathway rewritten: sibling answers (1790s, equator-to-pole, platinum-iridium) stripped, 1889/1960/rod grounded via idx 23 (now cited); consolidator: fact read verbatim from the page render this run

Text: The standard unit of time is the {{c1::second}}, now defined in terms of the frequency of radiation emitted by {{c2::cesium::element}} atoms when they pass between two particular states.
Back Extra:
Ex: one second is defined as the time for 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the cesium radiation.

Distinguish: the old definition was 1/86,400 of a mean solar day (24 h/day × 60 min/h × 60 s/min = 86,400 s/day).
verified_by: editor — Back Extra constants 9,192,631,770 and 1/86,400 match idx 26's context verbatim (text layer, EXACT grounding)

Text: The standard unit of mass is the {{c1::kilogram}} — defined as exactly the mass of a particular {{c2::platinum-iridium::alloy}} cylinder kept at the {{c3::International Bureau of Weights and Measures::institution}} near Paris.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: same alloy, different object — the 1889 meter standard was a platinum-iridium bar with engraved marks; the mass standard is a platinum-iridium cylinder.

Ex: for practical purposes, 1 kg weighs about 2.2 pounds on Earth.
verified_by: agent, read from page render this run; editor — 1889 meter-bar fact in Distinguish grounded via idx 23 (now cited)

Text: When dealing with atoms and molecules, mass is usually given in the {{c1::unified atomic mass unit (u or amu)}} rather than in kilograms.
Back Extra:
Ex: 1 u = 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

Why: atomic-scale masses are absurdly small in kilograms — a proton is about 10⁻²⁷ kg — so a matched unit is handier.
verified_by: agent, read from page render this run

Text: In the metric system, larger and smaller units are defined in multiples of {{c1::10::number}} from the standard unit, which makes calculation particularly easy.
Back Extra: Ex: the prefixes — centi-, kilo-, and the rest — attach to any unit, not just length: volume (centiliter), mass (kilogram), and so on.
verified_by: editor — prefix VALUES (kilo=1000, centi=1/100, milli=1/1000) stripped from Back Extra: they restated three sibling row cards' answers in prose (rule 25 back-leak, checks 16/27); consolidator: fact read verbatim from the page render this run

Text: In measurement, a unit is {{c1::the named amount a measurement is expressed in}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "The measurement of any quantity is made relative to a particular standard or unit, and this unit must be specified along with the numerical value of the quantity."

Distinguish: the unit is what you express results in (meters); the standard is the agreed physical reference that defines the unit exactly.
verified_by: lexicon in_source hit cleared: the p31 evidence quote 'unit (u or amu)' is the atomic-mass-unit sense, not the generic p29 sense Parker marked — downgraded to external per recipes §4b SENSE-CHECK

Text: In measurement, a standard is {{c1::the agreed physical reference defining a unit exactly}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "The measurement of any quantity is made relative to a particular standard or unit, and this unit must be specified along with the numerical value of the quantity."

Distinguish: the standard is the defining reference itself (the platinum-iridium kilogram cylinder near Paris); the unit is the named amount you measure in (the kilogram).

Text: A base quantity is {{c1::defined by its own standard, not other quantities}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Physical quantities can be divided into two categories: base quantities and derived quantities."

Distinguish: a derived quantity (like speed) is built from base quantities; a base quantity rests directly on a standard.

Why: scientists want the smallest set that fully describes the physical world — in the SI it turns out to be seven.
verified_by: long-blank warning cleared: 9 plain words is the floor that keeps the mandated discriminator (defined by its OWN standard, not from other quantities); consolidator: blank tightened 9->8 words, discriminator kept

Text: Derived quantities are {{c1::quantities defined in terms of the base quantities}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "All other quantities can be defined in terms of these seven base quantities, and hence are referred to as derived quantities."

Distinguish: a base quantity is defined by its own standard; a derived one is built from base quantities — e.g., speed = distance ÷ time.

Text: An operational definition is {{c1::a definition that specifies a rule or procedure}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "To define any quantity, whether base or derived, we can specify a rule or procedure, and this is called an operational definition."

Parts: operational — from "operation": the definition tells you which operations (steps) to carry out.

Text: An order-of-magnitude estimate is {{c1::a rough estimate rounded to powers of ten}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Such an estimate is called an order-of-magnitude estimate and can be accurate within a factor of 10, and often better."

Distinguish: the bare phrase "order of magnitude" is sometimes used to mean simply the power of 10 itself.

Formal: "A rough estimate can be made by rounding off all numbers to one significant figure and its power of 10, and after the calculation is made, again keeping only one significant figure."
verified_by: agent — authored plain definition checked against the mark's own context; anchor external (no lexicon_evidence entry for order_of_magnitud_estimat); Ex:/Formal: quote the context verbatim with the interleaved margin-box text removed; editor: verified_against normalized to PDF page p34 (book label 13) per block A/C convention; consolidator: verified_against cleared — an external-anchor authored definition is by definition not page-verifiable and must reach the Vocabulary block (R35)

Text: In physics, the {{c1::dimensions}} of a quantity refer to {{c2::the type of base quantities/units composing it}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: units change with the measuring system (velocity: km/h, m/s, or mi/h); dimensions do not — velocity is always [L/T].

Cue: dimensions are written inside square brackets — [L] for a length, [T] for a time.
verified_by: agent — grounded verbatim in the §1-8 paragraph; velocity/[L]/[T] support sits in the mark's own context; editor: verified_against normalized to PDF page p37 (book label 16) per block A/C convention

Text: In physics, the dimensions of area are always {{c1::length squared — written [L²]}} — the units vary, not the dimensions.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: square meters, square feet, and cm² are all different units of area, and the dimensions behind every one of them are [L²].

Ex: a triangle's area formula and a circle's look different, yet both have the dimensions [L²].
